review:frontend.overall:
I reviewed site/targeting_app.js and site/targeting_template.html as they stood at 12:09 (both changed while I was reviewing; line numbers refer to that snapshot, which I copied to scratchpad/fe_review/). I checked them in the live preview at 375, 360 and 320 px and on desktop, and checked the numbers against output/targeting/site_data.json.

What holds up:
- Escaping of data strings in innerHTML is consistent.
- Null fields seen in the data (census fields, kalpi data) are guarded.
- Performance is fine: re-rendering the map takes about 2 ms, rankings 6 ms and the planner 5–8 ms per slider step.
- The only external requests are Google Fonts and cdnjs d3. Nothing uses `<a download>`.
- At 320, 360 and 375 px the stacked nav keeps the objective selector visible.

What fails:
- Critical: the objective switch is not carried through. Under "Deny Netanyahu 61", Arab locality profiles and the summary contradict themselves. Under "Change-bloc seats", the Segments page is blank.
- Critical: every literature citation is silently dropped. The Sources page lists only 7 official-data items.
- Major: several items under the accessibility and mobile lens. These cover keyboard focus loss, the skip link, unreadable chart text on phones, the map's touch trap and resize reset, near-invisible low-value map circles, and numbers in localities.csv written in scientific notation.

findings.issue:

findings.fix: Headers: `` with CSS `.thbtn{all:unset;cursor:pointer;font:inherit;text-transform:inherit}.thbtn:focus-visible{outline:3px solid var(--accent)}`. Native buttons handle Enter and Space. Restore focus after a rebuild: `const fc=document.activeElement?.dataset?.c; …render…; if(fc) t.querySelector(`button[data-c="${fc}"]`)?.focus();`. Render the view buttons, metric list and segment chips once in setup, then on change only toggle `aria-pressed`. findings.issue: Every resize event rebuilds the map from scratch, even when the size has not changed. On mobile, showing or hiding the URL bar while scrolling fires resize, so the map resets mid-use. The new map draws at identity while d3 keeps the old stored zoom, so the next pinch or wheel jumps to a stale, wrong position.
findings.evidence:
Live: zoomed to Gush Dan and selected Ramat Gan, then dispatched a resize with no size change.
- Before: the <g> transform was 'translate(-1622,-1917) scale(11.14)'.
- After: the <g> transform was null (the whole country is shown) but d3.zoomTransform(svg).k = 25.06, still stored on the element.

The selection survived.
findings.fix:
```js
let rt,lw=0,lh=0; window.addEventListener('resize',()=>{clearTimeout(rt);rt=setTimeout(()=>{const c=document.querySelector('.mapcol');if(!mapInit||(c.clientWidth===lw&&c.clientHeight===lh))return;const t=d3.zoomTransform(mapSvg.node()),ctr=mapProj.invert(t.invert([mapW/2,mapH/2])),k=t.k;mapInit=false;if(route==='map'){renderMap();const [cx,cy]=mapProj(ctr);mapSvg.call(mapZoom.transform,d3.zoomIdentity.translate(mapW/2,mapH/2).scale(k).translate(-cx,-cy));}},250);});
```
In initMap, set `lw=col.clientWidth; lh=col.clientHeight;` and call `mapSvg.property('__zoom', d3.zoomIdentity)` before `mapSvg.call(mapZoom)`.

review:numbers.overall: I recomputed every prose number I could from localities.csv, segments.csv, kalpi_all.parquet, marginal_values.csv, validation.json, sensitivity_summary.json and site_data.json (the embedded payload matches site_data.json and content.json exactly). Most numbers are right under the default change-led-government objective. These all check out: 86,395 persuadable voters (2.0%), 90,832 rescue voters, 4,404 net votes split 2,342 / 962 / 1,100, 0.12 seats, +0.21 pts, 0.48 per 10k, 64% / 46% concentration, the 1.4x turf ratio, -3,177 untargeted, Arab 56% vs 1%, Druze 6% and kibbutz 6%, the effTop list, about 91,000, 64% in the top 25, Beit Jann 7.19 per 1k, Daliyat 5.06, Isfiya 3.61, Tel Aviv 2.66, Haifa 1.64, and the Ra'am / RZP 78% and 41.9% repeat-election figures. Nearly all the segment counts, eligible voters, turnout, 2022 and 2026 camp shares and named-locality figures in the content match the data. Kalpi aggregates match the locality values exactly (eligible voters, turnout and all potentials). Segment totals add up to the national totals (6,788,804 eligible; 1,215 localities). Vote-weighted 2026 list shares match the forecast once it is converted to regular-station votes. The real problems are these. (1) The 'change-bloc seats' objective is broken on the Segments page and in the summary chart, because segments.csv has no change_seats columns. (2) Two localities carry the wrong English names from a bad override. (3) Several summary statements are hard-coded to the change_govt objective and become wrong under the other two objectives. (4) The seat conversion contradicts the forecast's own marginal values. (5) Some summary claims and headline tiles are contradicted by the data. (6) Some playbook content mixes in external or raw-turnout figures that conflict with the atlas's own numbers or model.

review:strategist.overall:
The playbook content is strong. Most of the segment playbooks read like a practitioner wrote them: they name the right messengers, set sensible don'ts on haredi and Likud turf, and handle Druze and Bedouin with care. But the site should not go to change-bloc leadership in its current state. Four problems would hurt it in the room or if it leaked:
(1) Switching to the 'Deny Netanyahu 61' objective makes the summary call Nazareth and Umm al-Fahm 'change-majority cities' to 'mobilise street by street'.
(2) The Arab-sector wording ('low-visibility coordination', 'blocking-partner', 'transport lever') is a legal and leak liability. It also contradicts the model, which scores Arab turnout as strongly negative under the default objective.
(3) The tier rule labels 18 of the 31 'Persuasion battlegrounds' wrongly. These include change-majority base towns such as Kfar Saba, Hod HaSharon, Ra'anana and Modi'in, and the site tells users not to run turnout work there.
(4) The Druze rankings come from 2022 home-village candidate votes. Beit Jann's 2022 Meretz vote becomes 64% for the Democrats, yet the summary features it as the best place to spend volunteer hours.
After those, the site needs four more fixes:
- Station lists a field team can deploy (addresses, neighbourhoods, a 2022-to-2026 station crosswalk) that do not favour stale-roll stations.
- A summary built on realistic contact capacity and supporter-ID GOTV. The current headline describes a campaign of about 3.2 million contacts, and persuasion and rescue get no contacts at the site's own 400,000 benchmark.
- Layers for coordinating the four lists and for volunteer hubs.
- Coverage of evacuees, Golan and Ghajar, new immigrants since 2022 and first-time voters.

findings.where: src/targeting_model.py:937-960; site/targeting_app.js:217 (summary 'Field work is a margin lever'), 888-891 (method §8 formula), 488 (rankings note)
findings.issue: The headline potential adds two separate saturation programmes in every station (35% of the roll for GOTV, plus another 35% for persuasion/rescue). The methodology formula and the executive summary describe a single 35% contact of positive-value turf.
findings.evidence: In the code, max(0,·) is applied to each mechanism separately and each one gets k_cap (0.35 × eligible_2026). Recomputed from kalpi_all.parquet: the 4,404 change_govt net votes need 1.01M GOTV contacts plus 2.55M persuasion/rescue contacts, i.e. 3.56M contacts or 49% of the 7.29M roll. The page formula, Σ_stations max(0, total value)·0.35·eligible, gives 3,640 net votes from 1.35M contacts. 48% of persuasion+rescue potential sits in stations where GOTV value is negative, and the turnout side-effect of those same door conversations is ignored, although by the model's own logic it is negative there. eff1k uses denominator c_gotv + 35% of the whole locality, which assumes two programmes. kalpi total_ve1k assumes one combined conversation. The planner caps each programme at 35% per station. The three are mutually inconsistent.
findings.fix: Pick one model and use it everywhere. (a) One combined conversation: value = gotv+pers+resc, potential = Σ max(0,total)·cap, efficiency per that cap. Or (b) two explicit programmes: report each programme's contacts and efficiency separately, state the 3.56M total in the summary, and either net the turnout effect of persuasion contacts in NB-majority turf or justify setting it to zero (e.g. Pons 2018 found no turnout effect). Rewrite the §8 formula and the summary sentence to match.

findings.issue: Rescue is valued as 0.05×0.60×(MV_change − MV_unaligned). The 40% of movers who, as the page itself states, go to a non-change viable list are silently valued at zero.
findings.evidence: Every non-change viable list has a negative change_govt marginal value (pp per 10k votes): Likud −0.46, Otzma −0.58, RZP −0.70, Shas −0.37, UTJ −0.26, Joint List −0.41, Ra'am −0.04. If the 40% go to a Likud-like list, the per-contact value is 0.05×(0.6×0.49 − 0.4×0.46 − 0.025) = 0.0043, against the code's 0.03×(0.49 − 0.025) = 0.014. That is a 3.2× overstatement, and rescue is 1,100 of the 4,404 headline net votes (25%). Under block_nb, Reservists' own MV is +0.25 because its passing cuts NB seats, so with 40% going to NB the value turns negative: 0.05×(0.6×0.59 − 0.4×0.57 − 0.20) < 0. The 5%-per-contact rate also has no field-experimental basis (Fredén 2017 is a survey experiment), yet it is 10× the per-target persuasion rate. The summary calls rescue 'the persuasion lever with the clearest payoff'.
findings.fix: Use ρ·[0.6·MV_change + 0.4·MV_alt − MV_src], with MV_alt taken from each list's lineage-implied second choice. Treat Reservists (P(pass)=0.20, its own MV matters) and Blue and White separately. Label the 5% as an assumption without experimental support and tone down the summary claim.

findings.issue: The 2026 transfer matrix T[s→j] = c_j(s)·G_j/S_s is not a flow matrix: its rows do not sum to 1. Before IPF, a 2022 vote is therefore weighted very differently depending on which party it went to.
findings.evidence: Sum over 2026 lists of T for each 2022 source: yesh_atid 0.576, jewish_home 0.79, balad 0.84, rzp 0.98, likud 1.02, utj 1.18, hadash_taal 1.19, blue_white 1.39, yisrael_beytenu 1.39, labor 1.50. So a Yesh Atid voter counts as 0.58 of a 2026 vote and a Labor voter as 1.50. IPF corrects national column totals but not this reweighting inside each locality. Normalising each source row to 1 and re-running IPF moves locality change-bloc share by 0.65 pp on average (vote-weighted) and by up to about 2 pp: Ramat HaSharon +1.6, Giv'at Shmuel −1.4, Sderot −1.4; segment means settlement_rz −2.2, religious_zionist −2.1, liberal_urban +1.0. The cause is that the lineage compositions leave out new voters and abstainers and do not match the size of each 2022 source.
findings.fix: Build a coherent national source×list flow matrix with abstention/new-voter rows and columns, raked to both 2022 source sizes and 2026 list totals, before applying it locally. At minimum, normalise each source row. Then re-run the model and the sensitivity analysis.

findings.issue: The projection 'backtest' is an in-sample fit, and it does not exercise the matrix used in production.
findings.evidence: The backtest uses the Kolot Nodedim 2021→2022 matrix, which was estimated by ecological inference from these same stations' 2021 and 2022 results. It also uses the true 2022 locality totals as IPF row margins. It is then compared with a uniform swing that has none of this information. Beating uniform swing (1.49 vs 1.77 pp) is close to guaranteed and says nothing about the 2026 run, which uses the judgement-based lineage matrix (M1) with no fitted counterpart. The brief presents the figure as validation of the 2026 method.
findings.fix: Run a real out-of-sample test. Options: project 2022 from 2021 with a lineage-style matrix built the way LINEAGE_2026 is (without 2022 data); fit the KN matrix on a random half of stations and score on the other half; or project 2021 from 2020 with an earlier matrix. Relabel the current number as an 'in-sample fit of uniform-rate allocation'.

findings.issue: Druze projections mechanically carry 2022 local-candidate votes into 2026 lists. These towns then lead the efficiency rankings and the summary's 'best value per volunteer-hour' finding.
findings.evidence: Beit Jann: Meretz 62% in 2022 (15% in 2021) becomes Democrats 64% and change bloc 87% in 2026. Daliyat al-Karmel: Blue and White 7% in 2021 and 55% in 2022. Kisra-Sumei: Likud 47% in 2021 and 10% in 2022. Among localities with ≥2,000 eligible, the top 7 by net votes per 100 hours are all Druze or Circassian (Beit Jann 5.75, Kafr Kama 5.12, Yanuh-Jat 5.06, … Tel Aviv 2.93 comes 8th). All are tiered 'Turnout engine'; Beit Jann and Daliyat rank 19th and 18th on potential. Druze openness is also inflated: mean 1.78, several localities at the 2.28 cap, because swings between candidates read as volatility. The §12 caveat exists, but tiers and the summary still recommend these towns.
findings.fix: For Druze localities, and any locality with 2021→2022 list swings above about 25 points, project from a multi-cycle or candidate-adjusted baseline. Give them a low-confidence flag or tier, add a sensitivity scenario, and soften the summary headline.

findings.issue: The turnout hump in the code does not match the methodology text or the source it cites, in exactly the turnout range where most of the potential sits.
findings.evidence: The page says the effect is 'close to zero above 80%'. The code gives 0.73 pp per conversation at 80%, 0.49 at 85% and 0.34 at 90% (including spillover). The cited D3-F03 reports CACE 6.2 (30–50%), 1.4 (50–70%) and 0.6 (≥70%, not significant), so the ≥70% band is about 10% of the peak. In the code the 70–80% band is 33–41% of the peak. Recomputed: 71% of eligible voters live in stations with resident turnout ≥0.70; 57% of change_govt GOTV potential comes from those stations and 31% from stations above 0.80. The sensitivity set has a 'flat' scenario, which moves in the opposite direction, but nothing matching D3-F03's steepness.
findings.fix: Either set multipliers proportional to D3-F03 (softened if desired, citing Bhatti et al.) or describe the curve honestly as a deliberately softened prior. Add a 'steep hump' scenario and correct the prose ('1.5 at 30–55%' is also wrong: 1.2 at 30%, 1.5 only at 42.5%, 1.15 at 55%).

findings.issue: Efficiency and per-hour units are inconsistent and mislabelled.
findings.evidence: (a) eff1k = potential/(GOTV contacts + 35% of the whole locality), counted per roll entry including people abroad, with the value already multiplied by (1−abroad). The rankings text calls it 'per 1,000 completed contacts on the locality's positive-value turf'. (b) per100h multiplies that per-roll-entry value by 'completed contacts per hour', so residents abroad are penalised twice (−4% to −13% by segment). The planner budget is labelled 'completed contacts' but uses the same per-roll-entry values, and the supporter-list units apply (1−abroad) to both capacity and value. (c) The rates of 8 (urban) and 11 (dense) completed contacts per hour contradict the code's own anchor: 6–15 doors/hour × about 1/3 answering = 2–5. Per-hour figures are therefore inflated 2–4×, and the 11-vs-5 dense/rural ratio has no stated basis.
findings.fix: Define a contact as a completed conversation. Drop reach from the per-contact value and apply it to capacity instead (cap = 0.35 × resident roll). Set contact rates to 2–5 per hour or cite a source. Fix the labels.

findings.issue: The 'Change voters who stayed home' metric (an executive-summary tile, a rankings column and a profile field) does not measure abstention, is not net, and is not a floor.
findings.evidence: It is computed as (2021 C votes/eligible − 2022 C votes/eligible) × 2022 eligible, clipped at 0 per locality. Nationally, regular-station change-camp votes fell only 16k (1,645,915 → 1,629,868), but the tile shows 74,049; without clipping the sum is 62,643. The figure mostly reflects 3.2% roll growth, per-locality clipping, and C→R switching (New Hope 2021 is coded C and its voters returned to Likud in 2022). It is not people staying home.
findings.fix: Estimate change-camp→abstention flows from the Kolot Nodedim 2021→2022 matrix (which includes abstention), allocated locally. Otherwise relabel it as 'fall in change-camp share of the roll, 2021→22, in votes' and drop 'net' and 'floor'.

findings.issue: The envelope add-back takes D2-F04's all-locality district averages and applies them to Jewish and mixed localities only.
findings.evidence: The district figures in D2-F04 average in Arab localities at 2.9 points. As applied, implied envelopes total 416,780 against an actual 462,807 (−10%). The Jewish/mixed average is 6.6% against IDI's 7.5%. Jewish localities in the North get 5.9% and in Haifa district 6.2%, where backing out the Arab 2.9 implies about 8–9 points. Resident turnout in northern Jewish towns is understated by roughly 2–3 points, so their hump multiplier is about 10% too high (Haifa, ranked #2; Karmiel; Nahariya; the Krayot).
findings.fix: Compute Jewish add-back per district as (district total − Arab eligible×0.029)/Jewish eligible, and check that the total reproduces 462,807.

findings.issue: The openness index is validated on one quantity and applied to another, and its mapping to a multiplier is undocumented.
findings.evidence: The validation target is absolute residual right-camp share movement, which grows with the size of the soft vote. Balance and footprint are partly size measures. The index then multiplies the soft-NB share, which is also a size measure, so NB share is counted twice. The mapping exp(0.30·z), clipped to [0.4, 2.5] and renormalised over all localities including Arab ones (where balance is high and the index was never validated), does not appear on the methodology page or in the sensitivity runs. The effect is damped: persuadable-voter rankings with and without openness correlate at Spearman 0.98 (top-20 overlap 18/20), so the prominent validation table has little effect on outputs. The chosen spec is the best of 6 on the same 2 folds (0.381 vs 0.379). Robustness checks I ran were fine: sampling noise does not drive the Spearman (partial 0.45/0.29), and the segment-shrinkage leakage is negligible.
findings.fix: Validate on movement relative to NB share (or logit change). Calibrate the 0.30 slope from the folds. Document the mapping, add it to the sensitivity runs, and normalise only over validated localities.

findings.issue: Several methodology statements and code comments say something different from what the code does.
findings.evidence: 'Set to zero in Arab localities': arab_christian is ×0.3. The footprint list leaves out YB 2019a, Kadima 2013 and Am Shalem 2013, which the code includes. 'Rescaled within their locality so that they add up to the locality projection': vote-weighted station sums deviate by up to 1.2 pp (Haifa change +1.19; Akko NB +1.66; Jerusalem ±0.95). 'Diminishing returns are handled in the planner': the planner only orders stations into 4 capacity tranches, and value per contact is constant within a station. The module docstring still describes a logit-scale turnout effect, a segment-tilted marginal voter and a 2013–2021→2022 openness fit, none of which the code does. The CROSS_PRESSURE comment says 2.5%; the actual figure is 2.04%.
findings.fix: Bring the text and comments in line with the code, or add an exact per-list rescale for stations.

findings.issue: Camp and bloc coding has small inconsistencies.
findings.evidence: Gesher 2019a is in C_PARTIES (camp C) and also in the SOFT_RIGHT footprint. The page's camp definition does not mention it, and the coding moves 1.75% of mostly Kulanu/Likud-type voters into C in the 2015→2019a volatility transition. In LETTERS, the contemporaneous bloc has Kulanu as 'un' in 2015 but 'nb' in 2019a, although Kahlon recommended Netanyahu after both elections, and YB 2019s as 'ch', although Liberman recommended no one in September 2019. That bloc field (v_nb/v_ch) is written but never used downstream, so these entries are inert. The letter mappings themselves check out against the expected shares.
findings.fix: Code Gesher 2019a as O or soft-right, or drop it from the 2015→2019a transition. Remove or fix the unused bloc field.

findings.issue: Supporter-list turnout units in the planner double count people already covered by area canvassing.
findings.evidence: Supporter capacity (sup × elig26 × p_change × 0.35 × (1−abroad)) is added on top of area-GOTV units for the same stations. At 100% identified, the same change supporters can be contacted under both. The value uses the locality-average hump lift, although identified supporters have above-average turnout propensity, and (1−abroad) is applied in both capacity and value.
findings.fix: Subtract supporter capacity from area units (or cap total contacts per station), and use a lower, high-propensity lift for identified supporters.

findings.issue: Sensitivity labels are misleading, and the scenarios miss the assumptions most likely to change the top 25.
findings.evidence: 'Persuasion ×4 (Pons-like)' gives about 1.2% switching per soft-NB conversation, roughly 0.1 switchers per 100 doors, against Pons's ~2.8 per 100 doors (P-F02). 'Cross-pressured 40%' is simply persuasion ×1.82, because RHO_PERSUADE is fixed at 0.003/0.22 when the module is imported. There are no scenarios for the projection matrix (M1), the Druze baseline (M3), the rescue destination (C2), the openness slope, or a steep hump (M4).
findings.fix: Relabel the two scenarios and add the missing ones.

findings.issue: Missing caveat: station-level turf selection favours stations whose low turnout is really phantom registrants.
findings.evidence: Station resident turnout uses the locality-average share of the roll abroad. Abroad and stale-address shares vary within localities, so stations whose low 2022 turnout comes from phantom registrants get a higher hump multiplier and an overstated reach. Both errors push in the same direction, inflating the summary's 'choosing stations yields N× per contact'. D2-F14 and D2-F15 flag this risk; §12 does not mention it.
findings.fix: Add the caveat. Proxy station-level abroad share with station turnout stability across 2019–2022 or CBS statistical-area data.

review:methodology.overall:
The data plumbing is solid. The letter mappings pass their share checks, and the exchange-rate machinery holds up: I re-ran the marginal-value calculation and its Monte Carlo SE is about 0.03 pp per 10k votes for change_govt and about 0.07 for block_nb, so Yashar vs YB and Ra'am vs Joint List are real differences. The openness validation survives noise and leakage checks, and the composition test is reported honestly.

The aggregation layer has two critical problems.
- **Potential:** the headline 4,404 net votes needs 3.56M contacts, about half the roll, not the 35% of positive-value turf the summary and §8 formula describe; the page's own formula gives 3,640.
- **Rescue:** the 40% of movers who go to non-change lists are valued at zero, so rescue (25% of potential) is overstated about 3×, and its sign can flip under the blocking objective.

Five major issues follow:
- The 2026 transfer matrix is not a flow matrix: source rows sum to 0.58–1.50, biasing locality projections by up to about 2 pp.
- The 'backtest' is an in-sample fit on a different matrix from the one used in production.
- Druze 2022 candidate effects drive the top efficiency ranks and a summary headline.
- The turnout hump does not match its cited source in the ≥70% band where 57% of GOTV potential sits.
- The efficiency and per-hour units are inconsistent (per roll entry vs per completed contact), with contact rates 2–4× the code's own anchor.

A sixth major one is the 'stayed home' tile: it is mislabelled and is not an abstention measure.

After fixing C1, C2 and M1–M3, the rankings should be re-run before the summary's quantitative claims are relied on.

The top 7 by per100h among localities with ≥2k eligible are all Druze or Circassian, with Tel Aviv 8th. Druze openness averages 1.74 and several towns sit at the 2.28 cap. Recommended fix: a low-confidence flag or multi-cycle baseline for localities with large swings, plus a scenario. Severity minor to major.

Confirmed. lift(p) = 2.34 pp at 30%, 2.93 at 42.5%, 2.24 at 55%, 1.21 at 70%, 0.73 at 80%, 0.49 at 85% and 0.34 at 90%. The 70-80% band is 25-41% of the peak, against about 10% in D3-F03 (0.6/6.2). Softening the curve can be defended (the research desk recommended a soft multiplier following Bhatti et al., and only two studies fall in the ≥70% bin), but the description must match the code and a steep scenario should be added.

Confirmed. (a) eff1k = potential/(c_gotv + 0.35·whole-locality elig) and the value includes reach=(1-abroad), yet the rankings text says 'per 1,000 completed contacts on the locality's positive-value turf'. (b) per100h multiplies a per-roll-entry value by 'completed contacts per hour', so (1-abroad) is applied when it should not be (-4% to -13% by segment). Supporter units in the planner apply (1-abroad) to both cap (JS line 787) and VS (build_targeting_site.py vsup), a true double count. (c) The CONTACTS_PER_HOUR comment gives its anchor as 6-15 doors/hour × ~1/3 answering, which is 2-5 completed contacts, but the values are 8 (urban) and 11 (dense). Absolute per-hour figures are therefore inflated about 2-4x, and the dense-versus-rural ratio has no stated basis. Each piece is small, but the labels and units are wrong.
